title: Rate limits double as the whitelist: a venue with no configured limit is simply unusable
content:
A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.2.2.1.2.1.2.2.1.2 states it outright for deposits, and A...2.2.2.2 repeats it for withdrawals: "The rate limit is keyed to the specific `token` through `makeAssetKey`, and its available amount is decreased by the deposited `amount`. **This rate limit also serves as the whitelist, since only vaults with a configured rate limit can be used.**"

The elegance is in the collapse of two controls into one. A conventional design needs an allowlist mapping *and* a limits mapping, which can disagree — a venue can be allowlisted with no limit set, or limited but not allowlisted, and reconciling them is a standing source of bugs. Here there is a single source of truth: an unconfigured key yields zero available allowance, and the decrement reverts. Not-configured and not-permitted are the same state.

A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.2.2.1.2.1.2.2 confirms the framing in the section preamble: "each vault is whitelisted through its configured `RateLimits`."

The operational consequence is that **granting access and sizing access are the same governance act**. There is no way to approve a counterparty in principle without also deciding how much may flow to it, which forces the sizing question to be answered at onboarding rather than deferred.

The corresponding exposure is that revocation and throttling are also the same act — setting a limit to zero is how a venue is de-listed — so the audit trail cannot distinguish "we removed this counterparty" from "we temporarily throttled it to nothing." Intent has to be recovered from the Artifact, not from chain state.
description: Because every ERC-4626 operation decrements a token-keyed limit that reverts when insufficient, an unconfigured limit is a zero allowance — permissioning and throttling collapse into one mechanism.
